opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. Look, throughout human history we've basically had this strategy for dealing with powerful new technology, and it's worked remarkably well: we invent something, we screw up, and then we learn from the mistakes. We invented fire, burned down some houses, and then we invented the fire extinguisher and the fire department. We invented the automobile, lots of people died, and then we came up with seatbelts, airbags, traffic lights, and driver's licenses. It's this reactive, trial-and-error approach, and it's served us beautifully.

But that strategy has a hidden assumption baked into it, which is that the mistakes are small enough that we survive them and get a chance to learn. Once the technology gets powerful enough, that assumption breaks down. With nuclear weapons, for instance, you really don't want to learn from your mistakes by having a global thermonuclear war and then saying, "Oops, let's do better next time." There might not be a next time.

Artificial superintelligence is the extreme case of this, because by definition we're talking about something that's smarter than us across the board. If we lose control of something like that, it's not like a car crash where you pull the wreckage off the road, analyze what went wrong, and update the regulations. Once something vastly more capable than you is pursuing goals that aren't aligned with yours, you may simply never get the chance to correct course. It's a one-shot game. You have to get it right the first time.

So we have to shift from reactive to proactive, from learning from mistakes to what I like to call safety engineering. When NASA sent astronauts to the moon, they didn't just launch and see what happened. They thought carefully in advance about everything that could go wrong, and that's why it went right. That's the mindset we need with AI. And frankly, what worries me today is that we're treating the most powerful technology ever with less caution than we treat sandwiches. A sandwich shop has to meet food safety standards before it can sell to the public, yet companies can race toward superintelligence with essentially no binding safety requirements at all. That's the part that needs to change, and it needs to change before the mistake, not after.

r001.rationale: It says that once technology becomes powerful enough, mistakes may leave no chance to learn or correct course, making reactive trial and error inadequate.

r002.rationale: It uses nuclear weapons as an example where learning after a mistake could mean global thermonuclear war, with no next time.

r003.rationale: It calls superintelligence the “extreme case” and describes the danger of losing control, but does not clearly compare its potential consequences with nuclear weapons.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. Look, throughout history, the way we've handled technology has basically been trial and error. We invented fire, and we burned down some houses, and then we invented the fire extinguisher. We invented cars, and a lot of people died in crashes, and then we invented the seatbelt and traffic lights and speed limits. That's worked remarkably well, because the mistakes were survivable. You could screw up, learn, and do better next time.

But that whole strategy rests on an assumption that nobody ever states out loud, which is that you get to make the mistake and still be around afterward to learn from it. And for a small number of technologies, that assumption just breaks. We figured this out with nuclear weapons. Nobody says, let's just have a few global thermonuclear wars and see what we learn. With engineered pandemics, same thing. You have to get it right the first time, because there's no second time.

Superintelligence is the most extreme case of this. If you build something that's smarter than us across the board, and it has goals that aren't aligned with ours, you don't get a do-over. It's not like a bug in a piece of software where you ship a patch next week. By definition, it's better than you at strategy, at persuasion, at technology, at everything you'd use to regain control. So the first serious mistake could also be the last one.

And there's a second reason, which is speed. Our learning-from-mistakes approach also assumes that the mistakes unfold on human timescales. You have years to notice the problem, hold hearings, pass regulations. With a system that can think and act far faster than we can, and copy itself, and improve itself, the gap between "something seems a bit off" and "it's too late" might be measured in days or hours, not decades.

So I think of it like this. In engineering, when the stakes are low, you iterate. When the stakes are high, like building a bridge or launching a rocket with people on it, you do safety engineering up front. You prove, as rigorously as you can, that it will work before you turn it on. With superintelligence, the stakes are literally everything, so we need that second mindset. And the honest truth is that we currently don't have the tools to make those guarantees, which is exactly why I think we shouldn't be racing to build it before we do.

r001.rationale: It says trial-and-error learning works when mistakes are survivable, but some technologies cross a point where there is no second chance; it calls superintelligence the most extreme case.

r002.rationale: It names nuclear weapons and says nobody can safely conduct a few global nuclear wars to learn from the mistakes.

r003.rationale: It describes misaligned superintelligence as the most extreme case, says losing control could make the first serious mistake the last, and frames the stakes as “literally everything,” communicating consequences beyond those of nuclear weapons.

astra-6.text:
Well, learning from mistakes works only if you survive the mistakes. With most technologies, we’ve had that luxury. A bridge collapses, we figure out what went wrong, and we improve the engineering. It’s tragic, but we get another chance.

With artificial superintelligence, we’re talking about something that could be better than us at science, persuasion, strategy—potentially all the things we would use to regain control if something went wrong. So we can’t simply assume that we’ll deploy it, see what happens, and patch the problems afterward. A sufficiently serious mistake could leave us with no opportunity to fix it.

And this doesn’t require the AI to become evil or hate us. The concern is that it becomes extremely competent at pursuing goals that aren’t compatible with ours. If we can’t redirect it or shut it down, our usual process of trial and error breaks down. That’s why we need to establish that we can keep these systems safe before we hand them that kind of power.

r001.rationale: The response explains that sufficiently powerful ASI could make a mistake irreversible, so trial and error would no longer be an adequate safety strategy.

r003.rationale: The response describes severe consequences from losing control of ASI but does not compare them with nuclear weapons.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the traditional approach works when mistakes are survivable. We build a car, it crashes, we figure out what went wrong, and we make the next one safer. We’ve improved a lot of technologies that way, but it depends on getting another chance.

With artificial superintelligence, we could make a mistake that we don’t get to learn from. If we build something much smarter than us, with goals that conflict with ours, we can’t simply assume we’ll be able to switch it off or fix it afterward. Our ability to correct the mistake is precisely what could disappear.

So we need to do more of the learning before we hand over that kind of power. It’s not enough to make a system very capable and then hope that it behaves well. We need good reasons to believe we can keep it safe and under control before the consequences become irreversible.

r001.rationale: It says the usual learn-from-mistakes approach depends on getting another chance, and that with a much smarter system the consequences could be irreversible and correction could disappear.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention nuclear weapons.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the consequences of losing control of superintelligence with those of nuclear weapons.
